Officers
of'fi-serz
n. pl. (men appointed to a charge under authority; in Israel, scribes and marshals set with the judges; rendering Hebrew shoter, Greek huperetes)
From the Latin officium, a duty or service, from opus and facio, to do a work. Hebrew shoter is from a root meaning to write or set in order — the officers were originally the keepers of the registers, and so the men who summoned and marshalled.

Biblical Definition

Officers in Israel were subordinate appointees who made rule workable. Moses is told to gather seventy elders “whom thou knowest to be the elders of the people, and officers over them” (Numbers 11:16), so the office existed before Sinai's administration was complete. The law then makes it permanent alongside the judges: “Judges and officers shalt thou make thee in all thy gates, which the LORD thy God giveth thee, throughout thy tribes: and they shall judge the people with just judgment” (Deuteronomy 16:18). Two things are notable. Justice is to be local — in all thy gates, not in a capital only — and the standard is fixed by God rather than by the officers. David's reorganisation gives numbers: “six thousand were officers and judges” (1 Chronicles 23:4), a substantial civil service drawn from the Levites. The New Testament uses the word for the temple guard, and gives them one of the finest lines in the Gospels. Sent to arrest Jesus, they come back empty-handed, and to the Pharisees' demand for an explanation they answer: “Never man spake like this man” (John 7:46). Working men, sent to do a job, disarmed by preaching — and their report is a better Christology than their masters'.

Webster 1828 Definition

Men appointed under authority. Deuteronomy sets judges and officers in every gate with a fixed standard of justice; the temple officers sent to arrest Christ return with the confession, Never man spake like this man.

expand to see more

OFFICER, n. [Fr. officier, from L. officium, duty.] A person commissioned or authorized to perform any public duty.

2. A commissioned or non-commissioned man in military service.

3. One who holds an office; a person invested with authority in a particular department.

4. In Scripture, an inferior magistrate or attendant on a judge; judges and officers shalt thou make thee, Deut. 16.

5. Also, an attendant of the priests and elders; the officers sent to take him, John 7.

Key Scripture

Numbers 11:16 — "And the LORD said unto Moses, Gather unto me seventy men of the elders of Israel, whom thou knowest to be the elders of the people, and officers over them; and bring them unto the tabernacle of the congregation, that they may stand there with thee."

Deuteronomy 16:18 — "Judges and officers shalt thou make thee in all thy gates, which the LORD thy God giveth thee, throughout thy tribes: and they shall judge the people with just judgment."

1 Chronicles 23:4 — "Of which, twenty and four thousand were to set forward the work of the house of the LORD; and six thousand were officers and judges:"

John 7:46 — "The officers answered, Never man spake like this man."

Modern Corruption

Justice is centralised and professionalised, so that the local gate where Deuteronomy set it disappears — and the officers' honest testimony in John 7 is treated as naivety rather than as evidence.

expand to see more

Deuteronomy 16:18 puts judges and officers in all thy gates, which is to say justice was to be administered where people lived, by men their neighbours knew, under a standard none of them wrote. This is a real political principle and it has been steadily eroded wherever judgment migrates upward to distant and unaccountable bodies. Scripture's own guardrails follow immediately: no wresting of judgment, no respect of persons, no taking of a gift, because a gift blinds the eyes of the wise (Deuteronomy 16:19). The safeguard is not that officers are good men but that the rule they administer is not theirs and the people they answer to are near.

The principle to recover is in the officers' report. The Pharisees answer them with contempt — Are ye also deceived? have any of the rulers or of the Pharisees believed on him? — and the argument is entirely from credentials. The officers had offered evidence: they had heard him. Nicodemus then asks whether the law judges a man before it hears him, and is dismissed with a sneer about Galilee. The whole exchange is a study in how learned men insulate themselves from testimony they do not want, and how God is pleased to put a true confession in the mouth of the men sent to do the arresting.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew shoter is an officer, originally a scribe or register-keeper, hence a marshal who summons and orders. Greek huperetes is an under-rower, an attendant serving a superior.

expand to see more

Hebrew shoter (H7860) — an officer, overseer, marshal; from a root meaning to write or set in order.

Hebrew shophet (H8199) — a judge; the office set beside the officers in Deuteronomy 16:18.

Hebrew saris (H5631) — a court officer or chamberlain; Potiphar was such an officer of Pharaoh.

Greek huperetes (G5257) — an under-rower, an attendant; the temple officers of John 7:46.

Greek praktor (G4233) — an officer who exacts payment; the officer of Luke 12:58.

Usage

"Of officers appointed with the elders: elders of the people, and officers over them (Numbers 11:16)."

"Of justice set in every gate: judges and officers shalt thou make thee in all thy gates (Deuteronomy 16:18)."

"Of the arresting party's confession: never man spake like this man (John 7:46)."
